claim: An estimated 1.5 million people died from tuberculosis (TB) disease in 2020.
source: An estimated 1.5 million people died from tuberculosis (TB) disease in 2020, and TB is on course to retake its position as the largest cause of death by a single infectious agent (World Health Organisation, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organisation, 2021

claim: TB incidence is declining at a rate of 1–2% per annum.
source: Fuelled by ongoing transmission through exhaled or expectorated Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) bacteria, TB incidence is declining at a rate of 1–2% per annum, which is too slow given the risk and scale of mortality (World Health Organisation, 2021; Ragonnet et al., 2021), lifelong impairment (Dodd et al., 2021; Alene et al., 2021), poverty (Pedrazzoli et al., 2021), and macroeconomic consequences (Silva et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to World Health Organisation, 2021 and Ragonnet et al., 2021

claim: Most Mtb transmission in high-incidence settings remains unaccounted for, with less than 1-in-10 occurrences of TB explained by transmission from a known contact.
source: Problematically, most Mtb transmission in high-incidence settings remains unaccounted for (Dodd et al., 2021), with less than 1-in-10 occurrences of TB explained by transmission from a known contact (Glynn et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dodd et al., 2021 and Glynn et al., 2015

claim: The prevailing paradigm in TB policy held that symptoms and infectiousness commence simultaneously as part of 'active disease'.
source: In recent decades the prevailing paradigm in TB policy held that symptoms and infectiousness commence simultaneously as part of 'active disease' (World Health Organization, 2020; World Health Organisation, 1974; Houben et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to World Health Organization, 2020; World Health Organisation, 1974; Houben et al., 2019

claim: Passive case-finding has prevented deaths from TB but has not reduced incidence.
source: As a consequence, a policy of passive case-finding (Golub et al., 2005), in which individuals are expected to attend a health facility with TB-related symptoms before receiving diagnosis and treatment, was relied upon to prevent deaths from TB, which it has (World Health Organisation, 2021; Mandal et al., 2017), and reduce incidence by interrupting transmission, which it has not (World Health Organisation, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to World Health Organisation, 2021 and Mandal et al., 2017

claim: Not all individuals identified with bacteriologically confirmed TB report having symptoms such as cough at the time of screening for TB.
source: One important advance has been the finding in population surveys that not all individuals identified with bacteriologically confirmed TB report having symptoms such as cough at the time of screening for TB (Onozaki et al., 2015; Law et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Onozaki et al., 2015 and Law et al., 2020

claim: Sputum smear-positive individuals are 3–6 times more likely to be sources for TB disease in contacts compared to smear-negative individuals.
source: For example, molecular epidemiological studies show that sputum smear-positive individuals (i.e. Mtb detected via microscopy) are 3–6 times more likely to be sources for TB disease in contacts compared to smear-negative individuals (Behr et al., 1999; Hernández-Garduño et al., 2004; Tostmann et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Behr et al., 1999; Hernández-Garduño et al., 2004; Tostmann et al., 2008

claim: The presence of respiratory symptoms is not required for the exhalation of potentially Mtb-containing aerosols.
source: It is, however, increasingly clear that the presence of respiratory symptoms, such as a persistent cough, is not required for the exhalation of potentially Mtb-containing aerosols (Patterson and Wood, 2019; Asadi et al., 2019; Leung et al., 2020; Dinkele et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Patterson and Wood, 2019; Asadi et al., 2019; Leung et al., 2020; Dinkele et al., 2022

claim: Tidal breathing may contribute significantly to Mtb transmission.
source: Indeed, whilst recent empirical studies have suggested that tidal breathing may contribute significantly to Mtb transmission (Dinkele et al., 2022), exhalation of infectious aerosols appears unrelated to the presence of symptoms (Theron et al., 2020) or cough frequency (Williams et al., 2020) in TB patients.
evidence: Supported by citations to Dinkele et al., 2022; Theron et al., 2020; Williams et al., 2020

claim: Exhalation of infectious aerosols appears unrelated to the presence of symptoms or cough frequency in TB patients.
source: Indeed, whilst recent empirical studies have suggested that tidal breathing may contribute significantly to Mtb transmission (Dinkele et al., 2022), exhalation of infectious aerosols appears unrelated to the presence of symptoms (Theron et al., 2020) or cough frequency (Williams et al., 2020) in TB patients.
evidence: Supported by citations to Theron et al., 2020 and Williams et al., 2020

claim: About half of prevalent bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB disease is subclinical.
source: A recent review found that about half of prevalent bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB disease is subclinical (Frascella et al., 2021) and it is becoming increasingly apparent that subclinical TB can persist for a long period without progressing to clinical disease (Richards et al., 2021; Ku et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frascella et al., 2021

claim: Subclinical TB can persist for a long period without progressing to clinical disease.
source: A recent review found that about half of prevalent bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB disease is subclinical (Frascella et al., 2021) and it is becoming increasingly apparent that subclinical TB can persist for a long period without progressing to clinical disease (Richards et al., 2021; Ku et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Richards et al., 2021 and Ku et al., 2021

claim: Individuals with subclinical TB will not be identified by current passive case-finding strategies.
source: As individuals with subclinical TB will not be identified by current passive case-finding strategies, they will continue to contact susceptible individuals and, if infectious, transmit throughout their subclinical phase.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the definition of passive case-finding (symptom-dependent) and subclinical TB (no reported symptoms)

claim: Data on transmission potential from sputum smear-negative individuals relative to smear-positive have often been directly interpreted as relative infectiousness, which is incorrect.
source: In TB, data sources on the transmission potential from sputum smear-negative individuals relative to smear-positive (e.g. molecular epidemiological studies; Behr et al., 1999; Hernández-Garduño et al., 2004; Tostmann et al., 2008) have often been directly interpreted as relative infectiousness, which is incorrect (Kendall, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kendall, 2021

claim: Previous data on transmission potential actually provided a relative estimate of cumulative exposure rather than relative infectiousness per unit time.
source: Instead of representing the metric of interest, which is the potential for transmission per unit time for a particular group relative to a reference group (i.e. relative infectiousness), these data actually provided a relative estimate of cumulative exposure (as acknowledged by these studies' authors; Behr et al., 1999; Hernández-Garduño et al., 2004; Tostmann et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Behr et al., 1999; Hernández-Garduño et al., 2004; Tostmann et al., 2008

claim: Four studies were included for analysis: three prevalence surveys of TB disease with associated Mtb infection surveys in Viet Nam (2007), Bangladesh (2007), and the Philippines (1997) and a community-wide active case-finding trial in Viet Nam (2017).
source: Four studies were included for analysis: three prevalence surveys of TB disease with associated Mtb infection surveys in Viet Nam (2007) (Hoa et al., 2010), Bangladesh (2007) (Zaman et al., 2012), and the Philippines (1997) (Tupasi et al., 1999) and a community-wide active case-finding trial in Viet Nam (2017) (Marks et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hoa et al., 2010; Zaman et al., 2012; Tupasi et al., 1999; Marks et al., 2019

claim: The odds ratio for infection in members of a household with a clinical versus subclinical index case (irrespective of sputum smear status) was 1.2 (0.6–2.3, 95% confidence interval).
source: A mixed-effects meta-analysis across studies provides OR = 1.2 (0.6–2.3, 95% confidence interval [CI]).
evidence: Derived from statistical analysis of collected data across multiple studies

claim: The odds ratio for infection in members of a household with a sputum smear-positive versus a smear-negative index case (irrespective of symptoms) was 2.3 (1.3–3.9, 95% CI).
source: In contrast to the analysis by symptom status, evidence for a difference in cumulative infection was found by smear status, with OR = 2.3 (1.3–3.9, 95% CI), which is in line with previous estimates (Grzybowski et al., 1975).
evidence: Derived from statistical analysis of collected data and supported by citation to Grzybowski et al., 1975

claim: The estimated infectiousness of subclinical TB per unit time relative to clinical TB is 1.93 (0.62–6.18, 95% prediction interval).
source: The estimated infectiousness of subclinical TB per unit time relative to clinical TB is shown in Figure 2A, both for each study separately as well as the mixed-effects meta-analysed result across studies of 1.93 (0.62–6.18, 95% prediction interval [PrI]).
evidence: Derived from cumulative hazard model fitted to data and shown in Figure 2A

claim: The infectiousness per unit time of sputum smear-negative versus smear-positive TB is 0.26 (0.03–2.47, 95% PrI).
source: Figure 2B shows the analogous results for the infectiousness per unit time of sputum smear-negative versus smear-positive TB, with a summary value of 0.26 (0.03–2.47, 95% PrI).
evidence: Derived from cumulative hazard model fitted to data and shown in Figure 2B

claim: Data from 15 prevalence surveys where the proportion of subclinical and clinical TB was reported by sputum smear status were included.
source: Data from 15 prevalence surveys where the proportion of subclinical and clinical TB was reported by sputum smear status were included, detailed in Appendix 1—table 2.
evidence: Refers to data collected and detailed in Appendix 1—table 2

claim: The overall proportion of prevalent TB that is subclinical was 58% (29–82%, 95% PrI).
source: In this subset, the overall proportion of prevalent TB that is subclinical was 58% (29–82%, 95% PrI), whilst the proportion smear-positive was 33% (18–52%, 95% PrI) for subclinical TB and 53% (25–80%, 95% PrI) for clinical TB.
evidence: Derived from meta-analysis of prevalence survey data

claim: The proportion smear-positive was 33% (18–52%, 95% PrI) for subclinical TB.
source: In this subset, the overall proportion of prevalent TB that is subclinical was 58% (29–82%, 95% PrI), whilst the proportion smear-positive was 33% (18–52%, 95% PrI) for subclinical TB and 53% (25–80%, 95% PrI) for clinical TB.
evidence: Derived from meta-analysis of prevalence survey data

claim: The proportion smear-positive was 53% (25–80%, 95% PrI) for clinical TB.
source: In this subset, the overall proportion of prevalent TB that is subclinical was 58% (29–82%, 95% PrI), whilst the proportion smear-positive was 33% (18–52%, 95% PrI) for subclinical TB and 53% (25–80%, 95% PrI) for clinical TB.
evidence: Derived from meta-analysis of prevalence survey data

claim: 68% (27–92%, 95% PrI) of global Mtb transmission is estimated to come from prevalent subclinical TB.
source: As such we used a summary value for the included surveys as a global estimate. Figure 3D shows the results by country and globally, where 68% (27–92%, 95% PrI) of global Mtb transmission is estimated to come from prevalent subclinical TB, ranging from 45% (19–76%, 95% PrI) in Nigeria to 84% (60–95%, 95% PrI) in Mongolia.
evidence: Derived from combining estimates of relative infectiousness and prevalence data, shown in Figure 3D

claim: The contribution of subclinical TB to transmission ranges from 45% (19–76%, 95% PrI) in Nigeria to 84% (60–95%, 95% PrI) in Mongolia.
source: Figure 3D shows the results by country and globally, where 68% (27–92%, 95% PrI) of global Mtb transmission is estimated to come from prevalent subclinical TB, ranging from 45% (19–76%, 95% PrI) in Nigeria to 84% (60–95%, 95% PrI) in Mongolia.
evidence: Derived from combining estimates of relative infectiousness and prevalence data, shown in Figure 3D

claim: The 14 included countries represent around 85% of current global TB incidence.
source: The 14 included countries are a reasonable reflection of the geography and epidemiological characteristics of high TB burden countries in the WHO African, South-East Asia, and Western Pacific regions, which together represent around 85% of current global TB incidence (World Health Organisation, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organisation, 2021

claim: 36% of individuals likely transmitted Mtb before symptom onset, assuming a linear SNP mutation rate.
source: Our results are also in keeping with recent results from whole-genome sequencing (Xu et al., 2019) in which 36% of individuals likely transmitted Mtb before symptom onset, assuming a linear SNP mutation rate.
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2019

claim: Among children aged 6–10 years, those living with clinical, smear-positive TB, and those living with subclinical, smear-positive TB had similarly increased risks of TST positivity compared with those living without TB.
source: Using data from the 2007 Viet Nam prevalence survey, however, Nguyen et al., 2023 find that among children aged 6–10 years, those living with clinical, smear-positive TB, and those living with subclinical, smear-positive TB had similarly increased risks of TST positivity compared with those living without TB.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nguyen et al., 2023

claim: A recent small study from Uganda found no evidence of a difference in cumulative infection rates in household contacts of patients who did or did not report symptoms.
source: Moreover, a recent small study from Uganda found no evidence of a difference in cumulative infection rates in household contacts of patients who did or did not report symptoms (Baik et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baik et al., 2021

claim: Recent work on SARS-CoV-2 and malaria has shown how 'asymptomatic' or 'subpatent' infections can be important drivers of transmission.
source: More broadly, recent work on SARS-CoV-2 and malaria has similarly shown how 'asymptomatic' or 'subpatent' infections can be important drivers of transmission (Slater et al., 2019; Emery et al., 2020; Johansson et al., 2021), meaning a role for asymptomatic transmission would not be unique to TB.
evidence: Supported by citations to Slater et al., 2019; Emery et al., 2020; Johansson et al., 2021

claim: The studies screened a minimum of 252,000 individuals for bacteriologically confirmed TB disease and 63,000 individuals for Mtb infection.
source: Our estimates rely on studies which screened a minimum of 252,000 individuals for bacteriologically confirmed TB disease and 63,000 individuals for Mtb infection.
evidence: Refers to the scale of data collection in the included studies

claim: Symptom-independent TB screening and treatment policies can reduce TB burden at higher rates than usually seen under DOTS.
source: Our observation that reported symptoms are a poor proxy for infectiousness fits with historical and contemporary observations that symptom-independent TB screening and treatment policies can reduce TB burden at higher rates than usually seen under DOTS (Marks et al., 2019; Krivinka et al., 1974).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marks et al., 2019 and Krivinka et al., 1974

claim: Symptoms, in particular the classic TB symptom of cough, are not closely correlated to the amount of Mtb exhaled.
source: This is in keeping with increasing data showing that symptoms, in particular the classic TB symptom of cough, are not closely correlated to the amount of Mtb exhaled (Williams et al., 2020) and observations of other pathogens, including SARS-CoV-2 infection (Emery et al., 2020; Johansson et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Williams et al., 2020; Emery et al., 2020; Johansson et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020

claim: Earlier diagnosis (i.e. before symptom onset) will likely bring individual-level benefits in terms of mortality and extent of post-TB sequelae.
source: Whilst earlier diagnosis (i.e. before symptom onset) will likely bring individual-level benefits in terms of mortality and extent of post-TB sequelae (Allwood et al., 2019), the question of potential population benefits has hampered decisions from policymakers and funders on whether to invest resources in technologies and strategies that can identify subclinical TB.
evidence: Supported by citation to Allwood et al., 2019

claim: Around half of eligible adults in the general population are unable to produce sputum.
source: In addition, individuals are usually required to produce sputum as part of a confirmatory test, which around half of eligible adults in the general population are unable to do (Marks et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marks et al., 2019

claim: The subclinical phase represented between 27% and 63% of the time as a prevalent case.
source: To provide a value for the duration of infectiousness of subclinical relative to clinical index cases, we used the results from a recent study that estimated the durations of subclinical and clinical TB using a Bayesian analysis of prevalence and notification data (Ku et al., 2021). With the result that the subclinical phase represented between 27% and 63% of the time as a prevalent case, we used a duration of subclinical TB relative to clinical TB of 0.8 (0.4–1.7, 95% PoI).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ku et al., 2021

claim: A duration of subclinical TB relative to clinical TB of 0.8 (0.4–1.7, 95% PoI) was used in the analysis.
source: With the result that the subclinical phase represented between 27% and 63% of the time as a prevalent case, we used a duration of subclinical TB relative to clinical TB of 0.8 (0.4–1.7, 95% PoI).
evidence: Derived from data in Ku et al., 2021

claim: The data are from populations with a low prevalence of HIV co-infection.
source: Finally, our data are from populations with a low prevalence of HIV co-infection and the HIV status of individuals with TB was mostly unavailable, making a sub-analysis by HIV and antiretroviral (ART) status impossible.
evidence: Describes characteristics of the data collected

claim: An estimated two-thirds of people living with HIV have achieved effective viral suppression.
source: If they exist, any such differences by HIV-coinfection status are likely to be reduced by effective viral suppression, which an estimated two-thirds of people living with HIV have achieved (UNAIDS, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to UNAIDS, 2021

claim: Subclinical TB likely contributes substantially to transmission and needs to be diagnosed and treated for effective progress towards TB elimination.
source: Our results suggest that subclinical TB contributes substantially to transmission and needs to be diagnosed and treated for effective progress towards TB elimination.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study's data analysis showing 68% (27–92%, 95% PrI) of global transmission from subclinical TB

claim: If we are to meet EndTB targets for TB elimination, the TB community needs to develop technologies and strategies beyond passive case finding to address subclinical TB.
source: If we are to meet EndTB targets for TB elimination, the TB community needs to develop technologies and strategies beyond passive case finding to address subclinical TB.
evidence: Conclusion based on inference from study findings about subclinical TB's contribution to transmission

claim: The raw data and results of the analysis do not suggest subclinical TB is substantially less infectious than clinical TB.
source: Despite wide uncertainty intervals, the raw data, as well as the results of our analysis, do not suggest subclinical TB is substantially less infectious than clinical TB.
evidence: Based on interpretation of the study's data and statistical analysis

claim: Given the high prevalence of subclinical TB found in surveys, it is likely that subclinical TB contributes substantially to ongoing Mtb transmission in high-burden settings.
source: Given the high prevalence of subclinical TB found in surveys (Frascella et al., 2021), it is therefore likely that subclinical TB contributes substantially to ongoing Mtb transmission in high-burden settings.
evidence: Based on inference combining prevalence data from Frascella et al., 2021 with the study's infectiousness estimates

claim: The results were relatively robust to the sensitivities that were performed.
source: Our results were relatively robust to the sensitivities that were performed.
evidence: Based on comparison of primary analysis with multiple sensitivity analyses

claim: The qualitative results and conclusions remain unchanged across sensitivity analyses.
source: Our qualitative results and conclusions remain unchanged however.
evidence: Based on comparison of primary analysis with sensitivity analyses

claim: It is not possible to establish a transmission link between presumed index cases and infections amongst household contacts using molecular methods.
source: Although infection studies in household contacts have provided a novel window into transmission from subclinical individuals, it is not possible to establish a transmission link between presumed index cases and infections amongst household contacts using molecular methods (Kendall, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kendall, 2021

claim: Household contact studies are liable to biases.
source: Such household contact studies are therefore liable to biases and our study necessarily inherits such limitations.
evidence: Based on general knowledge about limitations of household contact study designs

claim: It is more likely that individuals will fluctuate between being subclinical and clinical.
source: An important limitation of our cumulative hazard model is the assumption that index cases only ever had the disease type they were diagnosed with during screening (e.g. sputum smear-positive, subclinical). Instead, it is more likely that individuals will fluctuate between being, for example, subclinical and clinical (Richards et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Richards et al., 2021

claim: Contact rates for subclinical and clinical individuals are likely to be similar inside the household.
source: For example, it is likely that, whilst inside the household the contact rates for subclinical and clinical individuals are likely to be similar, contact with individuals outside the household may differ (Glynn et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculation supported by citation to Glynn et al., 2020

claim: Contact with individuals outside the household may differ between subclinical and clinical individuals.
source: For example, it is likely that, whilst inside the household the contact rates for subclinical and clinical individuals are likely to be similar, contact with individuals outside the household may differ (Glynn et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculation supported by citation to Glynn et al., 2020

claim: Subclinical and clinical TB are part of a continuous spectrum.
source: In practice subclinical and clinical TB are part of a continuous spectrum and alternative definitions could be defined according to different criteria.
evidence: Based on general knowledge about TB disease progression

claim: The heterogeneity for the relative infectiousness of subclinical and smear-negative TB were low (I2 = 0% and I2 = 36%, respectively).
source: Whilst the heterogeneity for the relative infectiousness of subclinical and smear-negative TB were low (I2 = 0% and I2 = 36%, respectively), the heterogeneity for the proportion of prevalent TB that is subclinical and the proportions of subclinical and clinical TB that are smear-positive were high (I2 = 95%, I2 = 81% and I2 = 89%, respectively).
evidence: Statistical measures from meta-analyses of the data

claim: The heterogeneity for the proportion of prevalent TB that is subclinical and the proportions of subclinical and clinical TB that are smear-positive were high (I2 = 95%, I2 = 81% and I2 = 89%, respectively).
source: Whilst the heterogeneity for the relative infectiousness of subclinical and smear-negative TB were low (I2 = 0% and I2 = 36%, respectively), the heterogeneity for the proportion of prevalent TB that is subclinical and the proportions of subclinical and clinical TB that are smear-positive were high (I2 = 95%, I2 = 81% and I2 = 89%, respectively).
evidence: Statistical measures from meta-analyses of the data

claim: The subclinical TB presentation is likely affected by HIV in terms of duration and prevalence.
source: Whilst the subclinical TB presentation is likely affected by HIV in terms of duration and prevalence, it is unknown whether or by how much the relative differences in duration and prevalence between subclinical and clinical TB also change (Frascella et al., 2021; National Department of Health - South Africa, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frascella et al., 2021 and National Department of Health - South Africa, 2021

claim: It is unknown whether or by how much the relative differences in duration and prevalence between subclinical and clinical TB change with HIV co-infection.
source: Whilst the subclinical TB presentation is likely affected by HIV in terms of duration and prevalence, it is unknown whether or by how much the relative differences in duration and prevalence between subclinical and clinical TB also change (Frascella et al., 2021; National Department of Health - South Africa, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frascella et al., 2021 and National Department of Health - South Africa, 2021

claim: Symptom-independent TB screening and treatment policies have been observed to reduce TB burden at higher rates than usually seen under DOTS in historical and contemporary settings.
source: Our observation that reported symptoms are a poor proxy for infectiousness fits with historical and contemporary observations that symptom-independent TB screening and treatment policies can reduce TB burden at higher rates than usually seen under DOTS (Marks et al., 2019; Krivinka et al., 1974).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marks et al., 2019 and Krivinka et al., 1974

claim: An increased emphasis on symptom agnostic screening in the TB screening guidelines should be considered.
source: As our results show that subclinical TB likely contributes substantially to transmission, an increased emphasis on symptom agnostic screening in, for example, the TB screening guidelines (World Health Organization, 2021) should be considered, as should the inclusion of subclinical TB in the planned update of WHO case definitions.
evidence: Recommendation based on inference from study findings

claim: The inclusion of subclinical TB in the planned update of WHO case definitions should be considered.
source: As our results show that subclinical TB likely contributes substantially to transmission, an increased emphasis on symptom agnostic screening in, for example, the TB screening guidelines (World Health Organization, 2021) should be considered, as should the inclusion of subclinical TB in the planned update of WHO case definitions.
evidence: Recommendation based on inference from study findings

claim: Target Product Profiles for diagnostic tools should consider all infectious TB, regardless of whether individuals are experiencing or aware of symptoms.
source: Target Product Profiles for diagnostic tools should consider all infectious TB, regardless of whether individuals are experiencing or aware of symptoms, and interventions using such tools should be critically evaluated for their impact on Mtb transmission and cost-effectiveness.
evidence: Recommendation based on inference from study findings

claim: Symptom-independent tools exist for screening.
source: While symptom-independent tools exist for screening (Williams et al., 2020; Marks et al., 2019; Yoon et al., 2017; Madhani et al., 2020; Scriba et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2014), specificity, costs, and logistics remain an obstacle.
evidence: Supported by citations to Williams et al., 2020; Marks et al., 2019; Yoon et al., 2017; Madhani et al., 2020; Scriba et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2014

claim: Specificity, costs, and logistics remain an obstacle for symptom-independent screening tools.
source: While symptom-independent tools exist for screening (Williams et al., 2020; Marks et al., 2019; Yoon et al., 2017; Madhani et al., 2020; Scriba et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2014), specificity, costs, and logistics remain an obstacle.
evidence: Based on general knowledge about limitations of current screening tools

claim: Around half of eligible adults in the general population are unable to produce sputum as part of a confirmatory test.
source: In addition, individuals are usually required to produce sputum as part of a confirmatory test, which around half of eligible adults in the general population are unable to do (Marks et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marks et al., 2019

claim: Bio-aerosol measurements in TB may uncover additional infectious individuals whose sputum-based bacteriological test is negative.
source: Indeed, the advent of bio-aerosol measurements in TB may uncover additional infectious individuals whose sputum-based bacteriological test is negative, although these tools require validation in larger populations (Williams et al., 2020; Williams et al., 2014; Nathavitharana et al., 2022).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to Williams et al., 2020; Williams et al., 2014; Nathavitharana et al., 2022

claim: Bio-aerosol measurement tools require validation in larger populations.
source: Indeed, the advent of bio-aerosol measurements in TB may uncover additional infectious individuals whose sputum-based bacteriological test is negative, although these tools require validation in larger populations (Williams et al., 2020; Williams et al., 2014; Nathavitharana et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Williams et al., 2020; Williams et al., 2014; Nathavitharana et al., 2022

claim: Any bio-aerosol-positive, sputum-negative individuals are more likely to be subclinical.
source: Any bio-aerosol-positive, sputum-negative individuals are more likely to be subclinical and as such would mean we underestimated the contribution of subclinical TB to global Mtb transmission, even if their relative infectiousness may be lower than sputum-positive TB.
evidence: Based on inference about characteristics of bio-aerosol-positive, sputum-negative individuals

claim: If bio-aerosol-positive, sputum-negative individuals exist, the study would have underestimated the contribution of subclinical TB to global Mtb transmission.
source: Any bio-aerosol-positive, sputum-negative individuals are more likely to be subclinical and as such would mean we underestimated the contribution of subclinical TB to global Mtb transmission, even if their relative infectiousness may be lower than sputum-positive TB.
evidence: Based on inference about implications of bio-aerosol-positive, sputum-negative individuals

claim: Policymakers will need to decide on how to treat subclinical TB as new diagnostic approaches are developed.
source: As new diagnostic approaches are developed to capture the spectrum of TB disease, policymakers will need to decide on how to treat subclinical TB.
evidence: Based on inference about policy implications of new diagnostics

claim: More tailored approaches need to be developed and tested to prevent over- or undertreatment of individuals with subclinical TB.
source: In treatment, as in diagnosis, it is key that more tailored approaches are developed and tested so as to prevent over- or undertreatment of individuals with subclinical TB (Esmail et al., 2022).
evidence: Recommendation supported by citation to Esmail et al., 2022

claim: The study collated data on 414 index cases and 789 household contacts from three prevalence surveys and one case-finding trial.
source: We collated data on 414 index cases and 789 household contacts from three prevalence surveys (Bangladesh, the Philippines, and Viet Nam) and one case-finding trial in Viet Nam.
evidence: Description of data collected for the study

claim: The odds ratio for infection in a household with a clinical versus subclinical index case (irrespective of sputum smear status) was 1.2 (0.6–2.3, 95% confidence interval).
source: The odds ratio for infection in a household with a clinical versus subclinical index case (irrespective of sputum smear status) was 1.2 (0.6–2.3, 95% confidence interval).
evidence: Statistical result from data analysis

claim: Adjusting for duration of disease, the per-unit-time infectiousness of subclinical TB relative to clinical TB was 1.93 (0.62–6.18, 95% prediction interval).
source: Adjusting for duration of disease, we found a per-unit-time infectiousness of subclinical TB relative to clinical TB of 1.93 (0.62–6.18, 95% prediction interval [PrI]).
evidence: Statistical result from cumulative hazard model analysis

claim: Fourteen countries across Asia and Africa provided data on relative prevalence of subclinical and clinical TB.
source: Fourteen countries across Asia and Africa provided data on relative prevalence of subclinical and clinical TB, suggesting an estimated 68% (27–92%, 95% PrI) of global transmission is from subclinical TB.
evidence: Description of data sources used in the study
